summaryEn: Hoya reads the 1446 Hunminjeongeum Haerye book and discovers that the five basic Hangul consonants copy the shapes of the tongue, mouth, teeth and throat, while the basic vowels come from the sky, the earth and a person.
learningGoalsEn: Know how the five basic consonants ㄱ (g/k), ㄴ (n), ㅁ (m), ㅅ (s) and ㅇ (silent/ng) copy the shapes of the speech organs.
Understand that a stronger sound adds a stroke: ㄴ (n) → ㄷ (d/t) → ㅌ (t).
Know the three basic vowel shapes, the round dot, ㅡ (eu) and ㅣ (i), and what they copy (sky, earth, person).
Know that South Korea's spelling rules today count 24 basic letters (14 consonants, 10 vowels).
Read and recognize 입 (ip), 목구멍 (mokgumeong), 하늘 (haneul), 땅 (ttang), 사람 (saram), 자음 (jaeum) and 모음 (moeum).

origin.noteEn: Heritage history, researched from the sources listed on the Sources screen.

keywords.en: the Haerye edition (the book with explanations and examples)
giyeok, the letter for the g/k sound

scenes.narrationEn: Hoya finds a very special old book: the Hunminjeongeum Haerye edition from 1446. Haerye means explanations and examples. Inside, scholars explained how the letters were designed!

keyword.en: the Haerye edition (the book with explanations and examples)

scenes.artBrief: Hoya gently opens an old string-bound book with yellowed pages on a low table; soft light glows from the pages (pages shown as faint lines, no readable text).

art.altEn: Hoya finds a very special old book, the Hunminjeongeum Haerye of 1446, lying open and glowing on a low table.

scenes.narrationEn: The first secret: the five basic consonants copy the shapes of the parts of the body we speak with. The old book says the letter {kw:jamo-g} copies the root of the tongue closing the throat. Hoya waves you over to look at the picture.

keyword.en: giyeok, the letter for the g/k sound

scenes.artBrief: Simple friendly side-view diagram of a head with the root of the tongue closing the throat, drawn in soft colors, as the old book describes; Hoya points at it with his tail. The app overlays the letter; no text in the image.

art.altEn: Hoya waves beside a side-view picture of the mouth: the root of the tongue rises to close the throat, the shape behind the first letter.

scenes.captionEn: Giyeok: tongue root closing the throat

scenes.narrationEn: Now {kw:jamo-n}. The old book says it copies the tongue touching the upper gum. And {kw:jamo-m} copies the shape of the mouth. Hoya opens wide: "Ip!" That means mouth.
scenes.artBrief: Two small side-view diagrams: a tongue touching the upper gum, and a square-ish open mouth; Hoya opens his mouth wide in a funny face. No text in the image.

art.altEn: Two pictures: the tongue tip touching the upper gum, and a wide square mouth, while Hoya opens his own mouth wide.

scenes.captionEn: Nieun and mieum: tongue and mouth

scenes.narrationEn: {kw:jamo-s} is shaped like a tooth, and {kw:jamo-silent-ng} is shaped like the throat. So the five basic consonants, {kw:jamo-g} {kw:jamo-n} {kw:jamo-m} {kw:jamo-s} {kw:jamo-silent-ng}, each copy a part of the body that makes the sound.
scenes.artBrief: A playful row of five simple body-part icons (tongue root, tongue tip, mouth, tooth, round throat) like stepping stones, with Hoya hopping across them. No letters drawn.

art.altEn: Hoya hops across five stepping stones showing the tongue root, the tongue tip, the mouth, a tooth and the throat.

scenes.captionEn: Siot is like a tooth, ieung the throat

scenes.narrationEn: The second secret: when a sound is stronger, add a stroke! {kw:jamo-n} gets one more line and becomes {kw:jamo-d}, and one more line makes {kw:jamo-t}. Hoya draws them in the air with his tail.
scenes.artBrief: Hoya swishes his tail through the air leaving three glowing ribbon trails that grow from one bend to more lines (abstract ribbons; the app overlays nieun digeut tieut).

art.altEn: Hoya swishes his tail and leaves three glowing trails in the air, each with one more line than the last.

scenes.captionEn: Add a stroke for a stronger sound

scenes.narrationEn: The third secret: the vowels. A round dot copies the round sky, a flat line {kw:jamo-eu} copies the flat earth, and a standing line {kw:jamo-i} copies a person standing up.
scenes.artBrief: A landscape split into three: a round sun-like dot in the sky, a flat horizon of earth, and a child standing tall; Hoya stands beside the child. No text.

art.altEn: A round dot shining in the round sky, the flat earth and a child standing tall: sky, earth and person, the ideas behind three vowels.

scenes.captionEn: Vowels: sky, earth and a person

scenes.narrationEn: Put them together to make more vowels! {kw:jamo-i} and a dot join to make {kw:jamo-a}. With a few clever ideas, a handful of simple shapes grew into a whole set of letters.
scenes.artBrief: A tall standing stick and a small round pebble slide together like puzzle pieces while Hoya claps; sparkles show they fit. The app overlays the vowel; no text in the image.

art.altEn: A tall standing stick and a round pebble slide together and fit like puzzle pieces, and Hoya claps.

scenes.captionEn: Shapes join to make new vowels

scenes.narrationEn: Hangul began with 28 letters, and a few old ones are no longer used. South Korea's spelling rules today count 24 basic letters: 14 consonants and 10 vowels. Hoya cheers: "Jaeumgwa moeum, consonants and vowels!"
scenes.artBrief: Hoya juggling colorful blank tiles (14 of one color, 10 of another) in a sunny classroom; tiles are plain, with no letters printed on them.

art.altEn: Hoya juggles 24 blank tiles in a sunny classroom, 14 in one colour and 10 in another, like consonants and vowels.

checks.promptEn: What does the shape of {target} copy?
checks.explainEn: The Haerye says the letter mieum copies the shape of the mouth.

checks.promptEn: Which vowel shape copies a person standing up?
checks.explainEn: The standing line copies a person standing up. The round dot copies the sky, and the flat line copies the earth.

checks.promptEn: How do you get {target} from the letter nieun?
checks.explainEn: For a stronger sound, add a stroke: nieun gets a stroke and becomes digeut, and one more stroke makes tieut.

facts.claimEn: The Hunminjeongeum Haerye edition (1446) contains the Haerye, explanations and examples written by scholars, which reveal the principles used to make the letters.
facts.claimKo: 1446년에 만든 『훈민정음』 해례본에는 학자들이 쓴 해례(풀이와 용례)가 실려 있으며, 여기에 글자를 만든 원리가 밝혀져 있다.

sources.title: Hunminjeongum Manuscript
sources.quoteOrLocator: "The manuscript published in the ninth lunar month of 1446"; "It also contains the Haerye, or Commentaries, later explanations and examples by scholars of the Hall of Worthies"

sources.title: 국보 훈민정음 (訓民正音) — 국가유산 상세 정보 및 국가유산 설명
sources.quoteOrLocator: 국가유산 설명: "세종 28년(1446)에 만든 한문해설서 … 또한 한글의 제작원리도 확연하게 드러났다."

sources.title: 훈민정음 — 한국민족문화대백과사전
sources.quoteOrLocator: "해례편은 새로 만든 글자의 제자원리를 주로 밝히고, 그 음가 · 운용법 … 등을 자세히 설명한 부분이다."

facts.claimEn: The five basic consonant letters ㄱ, ㄴ, ㅁ, ㅅ, ㅇ were made by copying the shapes of the speech organs used to pronounce each sound.
facts.claimKo: 자음의 기본 글자 ㄱ, ㄴ, ㅁ, ㅅ, ㅇ 다섯 자는 각 소리를 낼 때의 발음 기관 모양을 본떠 만들었다.

sources.title: 훈민정음 28자모 — 한국민족문화대백과사전
sources.quoteOrLocator: "초성의 기본 문자인 'ㄱ, ㄴ, ㅁ, ㅅ, ㅇ'의 다섯 문자는 각 문자가 발음될 때의 발음 기관의 모양을 본떠 만들고"

sources.title: 알고 싶은 한글 — 강창석, 「제자 원리의 주요 특성과 배경」 (hangeul/short/004d)
sources.quoteOrLocator: "초성의 기본자는 발음 기관의 모양을 본따 만들고, 중성의 기본자는 천, 지, 인을 상형(象形)하였다."

sources.title: 한글 — 한국민족문화대백과사전
sources.quoteOrLocator: "이리하여 'ㄱ ㄴ ㅁ ㅅ ㅇ'의 다섯 글자를 만들어내고"

facts.claimEn: According to the Haerye, ㄱ copies the root of the tongue closing the throat, ㄴ the tongue touching the upper gum (Haerye wording: 象舌附上腭之形), ㅁ the shape of the mouth, ㅅ the shape of a tooth, and ㅇ the shape of the throat.
facts.claimKo: 해례에 따르면 ㄱ은 혀뿌리가 목구멍을 막는 모양(象舌根閉喉之形), ㄴ은 혀가 윗잇몸에 붙는 모양(象舌附上腭之形), ㅁ은 입 모양, ㅅ은 이 모양, ㅇ은 목구멍 모양을 본떴다.

sources.title: 훈민정음 28자모 — 한국민족문화대백과사전
sources.quoteOrLocator: "아음 ㄱ은 혀뿌리가 목구멍을 닫는 모양을 본뜬 것이고, 설음 ㄴ은 혀가 윗잇몸에 붙는 모양, 순음 ㅁ은 입의 모양, 치음 ㅅ은 이의 모양, 후음 ㅇ은 목구멍의 모양을 따른 것이다."

sources.title: 아음 — 한국민족문화대백과사전
sources.quoteOrLocator: "『훈민정음』 제자해에서는 'ㄱ'에 대하여 '혀뿌리가 목구멍을 막는 모양을 본떴다(象舌根閉喉之形).'라 하고"

sources.title: ㄴ (니은) — 한국민족문화대백과사전
sources.quoteOrLocator: 제자해: "혀끝이 윗 잇몸에 붙은 모양을 본떠서 ㄴ자를 만들었다(ㄴ 象舌附上腭之形)."

facts.claimEn: For sounds pronounced more strongly, a stroke was added to the basic letter, for example ㄴ → ㄷ → ㅌ.
facts.claimKo: 소리가 세게 나는 정도에 따라 기본 글자에 획을 더하였다. 예: ㄴ → ㄷ → ㅌ.

sources.title: 훈민정음 — 한국민족문화대백과사전
sources.quoteOrLocator: 제자해: "그 발음이 세게 나는('厲'로 표현) 정도에 따라 이 기본문자에 획을 더하여 제자한다고 하였다(보기, ㄴ→ㄷ→ㅌ)."

sources.title: 훈민정음 28자모 — 한국민족문화대백과사전
sources.quoteOrLocator: "나머지 9개의 글자는 기본 문자에 획을 한 번 또는 두 번 더하여 만들었으나"

sources.title: 알고 싶은 한글 — 강창석, 「제자 원리의 주요 특성과 배경」 (hangeul/short/004d)
sources.quoteOrLocator: "초성의 경우, 각 발음 위치별로 가장 약한 소리를 기본자의 대상으로 삼고, 나머지는 센 정도에 따라 거기에 획을 더하였다."

facts.claimEn: The three basic vowel letters copy heaven, earth and a person: · is round like heaven (the sky), ㅡ is flat like the earth, and ㅣ stands upright like a person.
facts.claimKo: 모음의 기본 글자 ·, ㅡ, ㅣ는 각각 하늘, 땅, 사람을 본떴다. ·는 둥근 하늘, ㅡ는 평평한 땅, ㅣ는 서 있는 사람의 모양이다.

sources.title: 훈민정음 28자모 — 한국민족문화대백과사전
sources.quoteOrLocator: "'ㆍ'는 하늘의 둥근 모양을 본뜬 것이고, 'ㅡ'는 땅의 평평한 모양, 'ㅣ'는 사람이 서 있는 모양을 따른 것이다."

sources.title: 훈민정음 — 한국민족문화대백과사전
sources.quoteOrLocator: 〈표 4〉 기본모음자: "· 天圓 / ㅡ 地平 / ㅣ 人立"; "천(天) · 지(地) · 인(人) 삼재를 상형하여 기본모음자 'ㆍ · ㅡ · ㅣ'를 제자"

sources.title: 알고 싶은 한글 — 강창석, 「제자 원리의 주요 특성과 배경」 (hangeul/short/004d)
sources.quoteOrLocator: "중성의 기본자는 천, 지, 인을 상형(象形)하였다."

facts.claimEn: The other vowels were made by combining the basic vowels; for example, ㅏ is made from ㅣ and ·.
facts.claimKo: 나머지 모음은 기본 모음을 어울러 만들었다. 예를 들어 ㅏ는 ㅣ와 ·가 어울린 것이다.

sources.title: 훈민정음 28자모 — 한국민족문화대백과사전
sources.quoteOrLocator: "'ㅗ'는 'ㆍ'와 'ㅡ'가 어울려서 이루어진 모양이며, 'ㅏ'는 'ㅣ'와 'ㆍ' … 가 어울려서 이루어진 것이다."

facts.claimEn: Hunminjeongeum began with 28 letters. Some of them, such as ㆆ, ㅿ and ·, are no longer used, and the current South Korean spelling rules (Hangeul Matchumbeop) set 24 basic letters: 14 consonants and 10 vowels. (North Korea's norms count 40 letters, because they also count double consonants and compound vowels.)
facts.claimKo: 훈민정음은 28자로 시작하였으나 ㆆ, ㅿ, · 등은 오늘날 쓰이지 않으며, 남한의 현행 한글 맞춤법은 한글 자모를 자음 14자와 모음 10자, 모두 24자로 정하고 있다. (북한의 규범은 겹자모까지 세어 40자이다.)

sources.title: 한국어 어문 규범 — 한글 맞춤법 (문화체육관광부 고시 제2017-12호) 제2장 제4항
sources.quoteOrLocator: 제4항: "한글 자모의 수는 스물넉 자로 하고, 그 순서와 이름은 다음과 같이 정한다." (ㄱ~ㅎ 14자, ㅏ~ㅣ 10자 나열)

sources.title: 표준국어대사전 — 표제어 '한글'
sources.quoteOrLocator: "1446년 반포될 당시에는 28자모(字母)였지만, 현행 한글 맞춤법에서는 24자모만 쓴다."

sources.title: 한글 사용에 남북한은 어떠한 차이가 있을까? (국립한글박물관 소식지 2018년 6월 제59호, 한글나누기1)
sources.quoteOrLocator: "남한은 기본 자모로 자음 'ㄱ, ㄴ, … ㅎ'의 14자와 모음 'ㅏ, ㅑ, … ㅣ'의 10자를 합쳐서 24자이다."

sources.title: 한글 — 한국민족문화대백과사전
sources.quoteOrLocator: "훈민정음 창제 당시의 28글자 가운데 지금 쓰이지 않는 'ㆆ, ㅿ, · (ᄋᆞ)'의 이름은 지어지지 않았고, 'ㅇ'과 'ㆁ'의 구별이 없어짐에 따라"

verification.notes: Third independent pass. Every cited URL for all 6 episodes (52 facts) was re-opened (UNESCO pages via Wayback copies when the live site resets connections) and quotes/locators were compared; the one exception is unesco.org/en/prizes/literacy (unreachable from here; its claim is now also backed by a Korean MCST press release). Eight minimal corrections were made: (1) Hangeul Day f3 no longer says 'Gregorian' (no cited source says the October 9 conversion was Gregorian; encykorea separates Julian/Gregorian only for 1932-45) and dates the October 29/28 observances; (2) f10 gains a third source (SBS 2018 with 국립한글박물관 curator); (3) Shapes scene 8, learning goal and f7 now say 'South Korea's spelling rules' count 24 (North Korea counts 40, 국립한글박물관 webzine 59); (4) Sejong scene 4/f4: 백성 is 'an old-fashioned word' with 표준국어대사전 added; (5) Jikji f8 quote no longer repeats a prize amount that differs between UNESCO page versions; (6) Tripitaka f6 wood and corner plates now have two further sources (정책브리핑; 박상진 wood-identification study); (8) Hangeul Day f9 gains a second source (문화체육관광부 press release); (7) Panjeon scene 8/f9: 'visitors cannot walk inside' replaced by 'visitor entry is restricted' because Haeinsa has run pre-booked tours inside Beopbojeon since June 2021. See hangul-printing.signoff.md.

authorNotes: The letter-shape explanations follow the Haerye's 'Jejahae' (제자해) as summarized by 한국민족문화대백과사전. The Haerye's yin-yang and five-elements philosophy is left out as too advanced. The add-a-stroke rule has exceptions (ㆁ, ㄹ, ㅿ, per 한국민족문화대백과사전), so the narration gives only the ㄴ→ㄷ→ㅌ example. The narration says 'a few old ones are no longer used' rather than naming exactly four, because ㆁ merged with ㅇ rather than disappearing. The 국립국어원 essay (004d/004g) notes that a few details of the design principle are still debated among scholars; the story keeps to the consensus points. Because illustrations must contain no text, the app should overlay the jamo (ㄱ, ㄴ, ㅏ and so on) as UI text on the scene art. REVISED: the shape descriptions now follow the Haerye wording exactly (ㄱ = root of the tongue closing the throat, 象舌根閉喉之形; ㄴ = tongue touching the upper gum, 象舌附上腭之形) and no longer promise a physical sensation or add modern phonetics ('back of the tongue blocks the throat', 'ridge behind the upper teeth' removed; narration and illustration). The summary now says 'five basic consonants' (only ㄱ ㄴ ㅁ ㅅ ㅇ copy speech organs; others add strokes). Scene 2 no longer lists 'lips' (the Haerye names tongue root, tongue, mouth, tooth, throat). Vocab 혀 removed because no scene shows it. FINAL PASS (3rd check): scene 8, goal 4 and f7 now say South Korea's spelling rules count 24 (North Korea's norms count 40). The ㄴ wording follows the standard Korean rendering of 象舌附上腭之形 ('tongue touching the upper gum'); the Chinese 上腭 literally means the upper palate/jaw, so no finer anatomical claim is made. REVIEW PASS (PR 1.8b): the old vowel arae-a is named 'the round dot' in learner text, never typed as a bare middle dot (screen readers skip it); the art overlay draws it. REVIEW FIX (PR 1.8b round 2): isolated jamo use the F-CNT-002 C6 sound-value table: ㄱ 'g/k' and ㄷ 'd/t' in keywords, the s2 keyword, the c3 target and the learning goals (ㅇ already 'silent/ng'). The goal glosses are modern reading aids; in the Haerye the throat letter ㅇ was the null letter and ng was written with the separate letter ㆁ, which the narration does not claim otherwise.
